after.worked_solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \frac{3\,\text{d}x}{|9x|\sqrt{(9x)^{2}-1}}=3\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|9x|\sqrt{(9x)^{2}-1}}.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $9x.$

So, let's substitute $u=9x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=9\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{9}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}3\int \frac{1}{|9x|\sqrt{(9x)^{2}-1}}\text{d}x & =3\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{9}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\frac{\text{arcsec}(9x)}{3}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $3{x}^{2}=(\sqrt{3}x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{3}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1+3{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{1+(\sqrt{3}x)^{2}}\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Tangent
content.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $3{x}^{2}=(\sqrt{3}x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{3}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1+3{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{1+(\sqrt{3}x)^{2}}\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{8-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{8\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/8)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/8}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/\sqrt{8})^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{\sqrt{8}})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{\sqrt{8}}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{8}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{8-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/\sqrt{8})^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (\sqrt{8}\,\text{d}u) \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}/2}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u{|}_{0}^{\sqrt{2}/2} \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{8-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{8\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/8)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/8}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/\sqrt{8})^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{\sqrt{8}})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{\sqrt{8}}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{8}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{8-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/\sqrt{8})^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (\sqrt{8}\,\text{d}u) \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}/2}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u{|}_{0}^{\sqrt{2}/2} \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$
